subject.gist: Residents built homes from discarded tires to live off-grid, endured a subdivision shutdown, and now teach others while still experimenting with growing food.

story.text: Greater World's residents share the wish to live off the grid in houses made from things other people throw away. Tires become thick walls, bottles bring in coloured light, and precious water gets used four times. Tom still marvels at walls giving back the sun's warmth on winter evenings. The community's history includes a shutdown as an illegal subdivision; Tom and his wife spend five years in a tiny hut while building their home. Today students come to learn, and food production remains an experiment. Tom's advice for taking these ideas elsewhere is practical: find someone in the county who wants to support them, and work with that person.

claims.text: The settlement is the Greater World Earthship Community.
The community occupies 633 acres.
There are about 70 Earthship homes here.
The state provided two acres for experimental architecture.
The experimental zone has no normal building restrictions.
16 years ago, when Tom came here, the community was shut down as an illegal subdivision
In the last 10 years everything switched: they realised this is a positive thing and let them do their thing
Reaching compliance took seven years.
The county supplies discarded bottles, tires and mulch.
Students built the complex over several years.
Cans reduce cement use; the cement matrix supplies strength.
The student complex will contain 30-foot fruit trees.
Simple Survival provides 15 gallons of hot water.
New designs maintain 71 degrees without outside heating or cooling.
Water serves washing, indoor plants, toilets and exterior landscaping.
We only get like 9 inches [of rain] a year here, so we have to save it and use it every way possible
The Global stays around 70 degrees.
The pump refills the toilet with 1.6 gallons of greywater.
Globals cost about $225 per square foot.
Tom and his wife built the hut in two months.
The original hut cost $2,500.
Keeping the hut under 120 square feet avoided a permit.
The couple lived in the hut for five years.
The hut is a 12 ft diameter, probably 14, 13 ft high
This building stays between 55 and 70 degrees; with a greenhouse in front it would stay between 65 and 70
The house walls are tires covered in adobe mud.
The children’s floor contains sand, adobe and straw.
The lined cell measures 20 by 40 feet, six deep.
The Duke wastewater containment system is permitted.
I never have to water any of this; I don't water this, but these weeds are actually treating sewage
The contained wastewater does not pollute groundwater.
$100 for the propane for my cooking stove
